Chapter 5: Rethinking Madness—Toward a More Compassionate Understanding.
Let’s pause and reconsider the way we usually think about madness. Most of the time, it’s seen as a disease—a kind of brain malfunction that needs to be fixed. But what if that’s just one piece of the puzzle? When we focus only on symptoms, it’s easy to forget the real, complicated lives behind those labels—the relationships, experiences, and personal meanings that truly shape who we are.
Imagine a man diagnosed with schizophrenia. He spends his days in a hospital, surrounded by professionals who see him mostly as a set of problems to manage. His thoughts get called “delusions,” his feelings are reduced to “symptoms.” No one really asks about his life, his dreams, or even what scares him. In that setting, he almost disappears—hidden behind a wall of medical language.
But what if madness isn’t just a disease? What if it’s actually a crisis of selfhood—a desperate attempt to make sense of a world that feels overwhelming or even threatening? When you look at it this way, psychosis can start to seem like a survival strategy—a way to cope with feelings or experiences that are just too much to bear.
Of course, that doesn’t mean the pain isn’t real. Madness can be incredibly tough to live with. But maybe, at least in part, it’s a deeply human response to life’s hardest challenges. Instead of just saying, “this person is sick,” we can see someone struggling to find meaning, to protect themselves, and to reconnect with the world around them.
And here’s the heart of the matter—this shift in perspective changes everything about how we help people who are suffering. Instead of only looking for symptoms to fix, we can start by listening to their story. We can try to understand what their experiences mean to them. It calls for real empathy, patience, and a genuine willingness to see the world through their eyes.
In real life, this means making space where people feel safe to share their stories, without worrying about being judged or pushed aside. It means remembering that, no matter how troubled someone seems, their story matters. And sometimes, it means being okay with uncertainty—accepting that some things just don’t have easy answers.
Healing isn’t a straight path. It takes courage to face painful truths, to rebuild trust, and to live with the unknown. But with the right support, it’s absolutely possible to move from feeling isolated and divided, to finding connection and a sense of wholeness again.
